scope: T-6 (split a/b/c), T-7 and L-5 -- the last open rows of the v5 metanarrative brief
headline: Ten packets, ten worker greens on the first attempt, for $0.151 of REAL billed spend. Three of the ten were corrections to what the numbers MEANT, and not one of those was findable by a test.

packets.note: Five times the tokens and four times the wall of its neighbours, for a packet that is not five times harder. The distinguishing feature is that its oracle reads the packet schema and asserts twenty required fields, so the worker had a much larger surface to satisfy at once. Cost still $0.035.
Green, and shipped a CLI that did nothing when run. See T-6e: the defect was in the ORACLE's reach, not the worker's work.
The corrective packet. Its oracle drives the script through subprocess rather than importing it, which is the only way the defect was visible.
The owner's correction, made into a packet. Three oracles (build 18, worse 30, kinds 20) -- the largest oracle surface of the session, for the smallest code change.

The session's only non-green step, and it was the coordinator's: starts_red named two of the three oracles the packet turned red, so prepare refused at the cold gate. Caught BEFORE any worker ran -- zero worker spend, one packet edit, no change to starting_commit. The worker itself was still green on its first and only attempt.

Seven oracles red at the starting commit, all seven declared. The largest oracle surface of the session (200 tests across nine files) for a rename of two keys -- which is the correct ratio when the defect is what a name means.

reference_patch_cost.question: Section 7 asks how long the coordinator spends writing throwaway solutions per packet, because that is the number that decides whether the cheap tier pays for itself.
reference_patch_cost.coordinator_turns_per_reference: roughly one -- each was a single edit written straight from the packet's own purpose text
reference_patch_cost.reading: Seven references, seven first-try greens against oracles written independently by seven different fresh authors. Writing the reference is the act that proves the packet's purpose text is sufficient to satisfy the oracle, and it costs about one coordinator turn. It also caught nothing about T-6d's missing entry point -- because the reference HAD one, and the oracle never ran either as a command. A reference proves the packet is satisfiable; it does not prove the oracle is asking the right question.
reference_patch_cost.caveat: This measures the reference, not the worker. The worker's own solution is what shipped in all five cases; the reference was never merged.

frontier_turns.explanation: One coordinator session produced all five packets, five oracles by subagent, five reference patches, the protected-paths gate fix (#83) and this scorecard. A per-packet frontier turn count cannot be extracted from it honestly. What can be said: the per-packet coordinator work was freeze, validate, dispatch, merge-preview, merge -- five tool-driven steps with no judgement calls after the packet was written, and the packet plus its reference was the only part that took thinking.
frontier_turns.comparison_to_v5_P1: v5-P1 spent 9 frontier turns and $197 of coordinator session across SEVEN dispatches to get one green run. This session got five green runs for $0.083 of worker spend, and the coordinator's per-packet share of the work fell to a fixed, mechanical sequence.

findings: THE UNITS WERE WRONG, AND ONLY A HUMAN CAUGHT IT. The scorecard summed an imputed list price with real metered spend and called it a total -- $241.43, of which eleven cents was money. Every gate, every oracle and the merge-preview were green throughout, because the mistake was in what the numbers MEANT, and the oracles' author shared the misunderstanding. This is the clearest limit of the loop found so far: it verifies that code does what the packet says, and cannot verify that the packet is asking for the right thing. Fixed in #91.

THE ONE THAT MATTERS: T-6d passed 31 tests and shipped a CLI that did nothing when you ran it. Every test called main(argv) in process; the module had no __main__ block, so `python release_scorecard.py --release ... --out ...` exited 0 and wrote nothing. A missing required flag also defaulted silently to None, which would have filed a scorecard naming no release at all. Found by RUNNING the command on real data, not by reading the green suite. The defect was in the oracle's reach, not the worker's work -- the coordinator asked for a command and then wrote a brief that graded a function. T-6e closes both halves with an oracle that drives the script through subprocess.

FIVE FOR FIVE, FIRST ATTEMPT. No retry, no escalation, no rework round, and no hand step inside any of the five loops. Against D-8's rule this is five consecutive greens with zero escalations for mechanical_bulk.

The protected-paths CI gate from #79 was structurally red on EVERY hybrid packet PR and had been merged over twice (#80, #82). Commit 1 of every freeze branch registers the packet oracle's command id under hybrid.commands, and agentops.dispatch.json is a protected path -- so the gate fired on the one change every packet must make. A gate red on every legitimate PR is one you learn to merge over, and then it is not there for the case it was built for. Fixed in #83 with the narrowest exemption that works, and PROVEN in production: #84 through #87 all passed it natively with no branch update and no merge-over-red.

Every one of the five references passed its independently-authored oracle on the first try. That is the strongest evidence yet that a packet's purpose text can carry the whole specification: five different fresh authors, given only a seam and a rationale, wrote oracles that a sixth independent implementation satisfied without negotiation.

The oracle authors' 'ambiguities I had to resolve' reports are worth more than the tests. Four of the five surfaced a real defect or open question that no gate would have caught: the packet schema's task_id pattern rejecting the L-5 id, gate_set and stop_conditions being absent from an additionalProperties:false schema, worker_totals([]) reporting cost_reported true for an empty corpus, and the turns_flat_cost_up comparison firing on rising turns.

T-6 was split three ways on the seam its oracle already had, exactly as M-10 was in Amendment 4. The split was free: three packets at $0.039 combined, each with a smaller oracle and a smaller failure surface than one packet would have had.
The corrective packet is the cheapest part of the whole exercise: $0.0144 and 79 seconds to fix a defect that 31 green tests could not see. That ratio is the argument for the loop.

THREE OF TEN PACKETS WERE CORRECTIONS TO MEANING, NOT TO CODE. T-8 (units), T-9 (scope) and T-10 (names) each fixed a number that was arithmetically correct and said the wrong thing. None was findable by a gate, an oracle, a read-trace or a merge-preview, because every one of those asks whether a number IS what the packet said -- never what it STANDS FOR. Two were caught by the owner reading a figure; one by the coordinator reading the tool's own output. That is the sharpest boundary of the loop this session found, and it is worth more than the ten greens.
debt: debt: the packet schema (templates/dispatch/hybrid/task-packet.schema.json) rejects an L-5 packet on two counts -- task_id pattern ^[A-Z0-9]+- does not admit 'v5.2-release-unit', and gate_set/stop_conditions are not declared under additionalProperties:false. Not blocking today because the live validator checks required fields by hand and no jsonschema is installed on the host (section 6), so the schema file is documentation that has drifted from what the loop accepts. Editing it is a protected-path hand-pass, which section 7 says to stop and report rather than do.

debt: worker_totals([]) returns cost_reported true, so a scorecard built with no receipts at all reports total_reliable true. Defensible ('nothing failed to report') but readable the wrong way. A consumer must read worker.attempts == 0 beside it. The T-6c oracle deliberately asserts the delegation rather than the value, so this can be resolved in worker_totals without touching build_scorecard.

debt: turns_flat_cost_up uses turns >= previous, so it also fires when turns RISE while cost rises -- arguably a false positive, since rising turns explain rising cost. The alternative reading is strict equality ('flat'). Specified consistently across brief, oracle and packet, so it is a decision to revisit rather than a bug.
debt: worker_totals does list() nothing, so attempts=len(receipts) raises on a generator. The spec says 'a list'; noted rather than fixed, because the shipped code is the measured artifact.

debt: devbox's /projects/dev/agentops checkout is 159 commits behind main with local modifications. The dispatch path does not use it (the coordinator runs from /tmp/v5-coordinator) but the hook symlinks point into it.

debt: release_scorecard.py has no --project filter, so a window over the global sink counts every repo's sessions. The live v5-T-series run's frontier half covers 4 sessions since 18:00Z -- this coordinator session plus whatever else ran in that window. Filter by the sink row's `project` field. Note this only ever distorts the usage-equivalent half; the billed figure comes from receipts and is unaffected.

cost_kinds_correction.what_was_wrong: This scorecard, and build_scorecard itself, reported cost_usd.total as frontier + worker. Those are not the same kind of number. The frontier figure is computed by log-session-cost.sh as tokens times a hardcoded 2025 list-price table: nothing meters it, and on a subscription plan it is never billed. The worker figure is OpenCode's own step-finish accounting of real metered API spend. The sum was an imputed list price added to real money, and the coordinator quoted it to the owner as though it were spend.
cost_kinds_correction.who_caught_it: The owner, in one sentence: sessions are usage, not actual API cost.
cost_kinds_correction.what_no_gate_could_see: Every gate was green, validate was fit on all three oracle fields, seven oracles passed, and the merge-preview passed -- for an artifact whose headline number was a category error. No test can catch a units mistake that the test author shares.
cost_kinds_correction.fixed_in: V5-T8 (#91): five keys, no sum, and a kinds oracle whose only job is that doubling the imputed half must not move the billed total.

the_honest_live_figures.reading: 12.4 cents of money was actually spent. The other figure is what the same tokens would have listed at, which is a comparison unit between releases and nothing else.

scope_correction.what_was_wrong: The Stop-hook sink is global -- it takes rows from every repo on the machine -- and release_scorecard.py had no way to scope to one. An agentops release counted whatever else ran in the same window. Separately, a scorecard recorded no window and no project, so two of them were not comparable and neither said so.
scope_correction.measured_effect: The same live window, unscoped: 4 sessions and a frontier usage-equivalent of $399.93. Scoped to project agentops: 1 session and $174.33. The unscoped figure was overcounting by 56%.
scope_correction.fixed_in: V5-T9 (#93): filter_by_project with exact matching (agentops must not match agentops-web), a --project flag, and a scope block recording project, since and until with all three keys always present.
scope_correction.why_it_is_the_same_bug_as_the_units: Both are a number that does not carry what it means. $241.43 did not say it was mostly imputed; $399.93 did not say it was mostly other repos. Neither was catchable by a test, because a test asserts what a number IS, not what it stands for.

naming_correction.what_was_wrong: #91 stopped the top-level block adding an imputed list price to real metered spend. But one level down, frontier_totals reported its figure as `cost_usd` and worker_totals reported its figure as `cost_usd` too -- two keys, same name, opposite meanings, directly beneath the block whose whole purpose was keeping them apart. Anyone printing scorecard['frontier']['cost_usd'] got $203.61 and every reason to read it as money.
naming_correction.also_fixed: worker_totals([]) reported cost_reported true -- 'nothing failed to report' -- which reads as a measured zero. With no receipts nothing was measured, so it now reports false, and a scorecard built with no receipts honestly reports total_reliable false.
naming_correction.fixed_in: V5-T10 (#95): frontier_totals -> usage_equivalent_usd, worker_totals -> billed_usd. Both still READ cost_usd from the sink row and the receipt, whose schemas own that spelling; only what they REPORT changed. worker_spend_from_receipt keeps cost_usd on purpose -- it mirrors the receipt and is a reader, not a reporter, with a named test saying so.
naming_correction.how_it_is_enforced: test_release_scorecard_naming.py asserts the two reporters' money-named key sets are disjoint, by a syntactic rule (a name ending _usd, or exactly cost_usd) rather than a maintained list, so a future `spend_usd` is caught without anyone updating the test -- and asserts each set is non-empty, so deleting a figure cannot pass it vacuously.
